work.title: The Second Part of King Henry the Sixth
work.author: William Shakespeare

lines.text: Fie on ambitions! Fie on myself, that have a sword and yet am ready to famish! These five days have I hid me in these woods and durst not peep out, for all the country is laid for me; but now am I so hungry that if I might have a lease of my life for a thousand years, I could stay no longer. Wherefore, o'er a brick wall have I climbed into this garden, to see if I can eat grass, or pick a sallet another while, which is not amiss to cool a man's stomach this hot weather. And I think this word "sallet" was born to do me good; for many a time, but for a sallet, my brain-pan had been cleft with a brown bill; and many a time, when I have been dry and bravely marching, it hath served me instead of a quart pot to drink in; and now the word "sallet" must serve me to feed on.

lines.text: Lord, who would live turmoiled in the court

lines.plainText: Contenteth me and worth a monarchy

lines.text: Or gather wealth, I care not with what envy;

lines.text: And sends the poor well pleased from my gate.

lines.text: Here's the lord of the soil come to seize me for a stray, for entering his fee-simple without leave.—Ah, villain, thou wilt betray me and get a thousand crowns of the King by carrying my head to him; but I'll make thee eat iron like an ostrich, and swallow my sword like a great pin, ere thou and I part.

lines.text: Why, rude companion, whatsoe'er thou be,

lines.text: I know thee not; why, then, should I betray thee?

lines.text: Is 't not enough to break into my garden
lines.plainText: Is 't not enough to break into my garden

lines.text: And, like a thief, to come to rob my grounds,
lines.plainText: And like a thief to come to rob my grounds

lines.text: Climbing my walls in spite of me the owner,
lines.plainText: Climbing my walls in spite of me the owner

lines.text: But thou wilt brave me with these saucy terms?
lines.plainText: But thou wilt brave me with these saucy terms

lines.text: Brave thee? Ay, by the best blood that ever was broached, and beard thee too. Look on me well: I have eat no meat these five days, yet come thou and thy five men, and if I do not leave you all as dead as a doornail, I pray God I may never eat grass more.

lines.text: Nay, it shall ne'er be said, while England stands,

lines.text: That Alexander Iden, an esquire of Kent,
lines.plainText: That Alexander Iden an esquire of Kent

lines.text: Took odds to combat a poor famished man.
lines.plainText: Took odds to combat a poor famished man

lines.text: Oppose thy steadfast-gazing eyes to mine,
lines.plainText: Oppose thy steadfastgazing eyes to mine

lines.text: See if thou canst outface me with thy looks.
lines.plainText: See if thou canst outface me with thy looks

lines.text: Set limb to limb and thou art far the lesser;
lines.plainText: Set limb to limb and thou art far the lesser

lines.text: Thy hand is but a finger to my fist,
lines.plainText: Thy hand is but a finger to my fist

lines.text: Thy leg a stick compared with this truncheon.
lines.plainText: Thy leg a stick compared with this truncheon

lines.text: My foot shall fight with all the strength thou hast;
lines.plainText: My foot shall fight with all the strength thou hast

lines.text: And if mine arm be heaved in the air,
lines.plainText: And if mine arm be heaved in the air

lines.plainText: Thy grave is digged already in the earth

lines.text: As for words, whose greatness answers words,

lines.text: By my valour, the most complete champion that ever I heard! Steel, if thou turn the edge, or cut not out the burly-boned clown in chines of beef ere thou sleep in thy sheath, I beseech God on my knees thou mayst be turned to hobnails.

lines.plainText: And hang thee o'er my tomb when I am dead

lines.text: Ne'er shall this blood be wiped from thy point,

lines.plainText: But thou shalt wear it as a herald's coat

lines.text: To emblaze the honour that thy master got.

lines.text: Iden, farewell, and be proud of thy victory. Tell Kent from me she hath lost her best man, and exhort all the world to be cowards; for I, that never feared any, am vanquished by famine, not by valour.
